title: Xenophon's Apology: why Socrates welcomed death as a just, well-lived life closed
summary: In Xenophon's account, Socrates refuses to rehearse a defence because he believes a lifetime of acting justly is the only real preparation. He sees death as preferable to the decay of old age, rejects servile pleading, and regards an unjust conviction as the shame of his accusers, not himself.

principles.text: The best defence is a whole life spent doing no wrong.
principles.quote: By a lifelong persistence in doing nothing wrong, and that I take to be the finest practice for his defence which a man could devise.

principles.text: The deepest pleasure comes from knowing you have lived holily and justly.
principles.quote: what can exceed the pleasure, which has been mine, of knowing that my whole life has been spent holily and justly?

principles.text: Old age erodes learning and memory, so a longer life is not automatically a better one.
principles.quote: I shall find myself slower to learn new lessons, and apter to forget the lessons I have learnt.

principles.text: Do not beg servilely for a diminished life; choose death over degrading supplication.
principles.quote: even so will I choose death rather than supplicate in servile sort for leave to live a little longer merely to gain a life impoverished in place of death.

principles.text: Death is natural and universal, so it should not be mourned as a calamity when it comes at a good time.
principles.quote: Do you not know that for many a long day, ever since I was born, sentence of death was passed upon me by nature?

principles.text: Suffering injustice disgraces the wrongdoer, not the innocent victim.
principles.quote: Nor yet again because I die innocently is that a reason why I should lower my crest, for that is a blot not upon me but upon those who condemned me.
